hints: Focus on what hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to a C=C bond, it completely breaks it and oxidises each end separately.
Remember the key rule, a $\text{C-H}$ on the double bond becomes a carboxylic acid ($\text{-COOH}$), while a C with no H and two alkyl groups becomes a ketone.
Look for the alkene where both carbons of the C=C each carry one H and different alkyl groups, so both sides can form different acids.
walkthrough:
**Recall oxidative cleavage rule**

Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) cleaves the C=C bond completely. Think of cutting the double bond in half and adding O to each carbon.

$$\text{R-CH=CH-R'} \rightarrow \text{R-COOH} + \text{R'-COOH}$$

**Link substitution to product type**

If an alkene carbon has one H, like $\text{R-CH=}$, it oxidises all the way to a carboxylic acid. If it has no H, like $\text{R}_2\text{C=}$, it stops at a ketone and cannot form an acid.

**Apply to the four structures**

Compound B is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH(CH}_3)_2$, or 4-methylpent-2-ene. Both C=C carbons have one H, so both become acids:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$
$$\text{=CHCH(CH}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$$
These are ethanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid, two different acids.

options.A: Structure A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3)\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$. The left C has H so gives $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, but the right C has two alkyl groups and no H so gives a ketone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(CH}_3)_2$. Only one acid is formed.
options.B: Structure B is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_3$. Both alkene carbons are of type R-CH=, so each is oxidised to a carboxylic acid. The products are $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$, which are two different carboxylic acids.
options.C: Cyclohexene is a cyclic alkene. Cleavage opens the ring but both ends stay joined in one molecule, giving hexanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$. This is a single dicarboxylic acid, not two different acids.
options.D: Structure D is $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH=CHCH(CH}_3)_2$, which is symmetrical. Both C=C carbons have H so both give acids, but both sides are identical and give two moles of the same acid, $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$. The question asks for two different acids.
